recommendations.regimenLabel: IV saline first, low-rate insulin, K+ replacement, VTE prophylaxis
steps: Aggressive IV 0.9% saline — fluid replacement is the priority (large deficits, replace gradually).
Low-rate IV insulin, started after fluids (or if ketonaemia/glucose not falling with fluids alone).
Replace potassium guided by levels; monitor osmolality fall (aim gradual to avoid cerebral oedema).
VTE prophylaxis (high thrombotic risk); find and treat the precipitant.
Monitor glucose, Na, K and neuro status closely.

drugRefs.dose: 0.5–1 L over the first hour, then titrated (aim gradual, e.g. positive balance 3–6 L by 12 h)
drugRefs.why: Fluid replacement is the cornerstone and alone lowers glucose/osmolality; correct gradually to avoid rapid osmotic shifts and cerebral oedema.

drugRefs.dose: 0.05 unit/kg/hour (start only after fluids, or if ketonaemia present / glucose not falling)
drugRefs.freq: continuous, titrated to gradual glucose fall (~4–6 mmol/L/h)
drugRefs.why: Lower rate than DKA because fluids do much of the work; premature/high-dose insulin causes dangerous rapid osmotic shifts.

drugRefs.dose: add per serum K⁺ (e.g. 40 mmol/L when K⁺ 3.5–5.5)
drugRefs.why: Insulin and rehydration drive K⁺ intracellularly; replace once K⁺ <5.5 mmol/L with adequate urine output, withhold if >5.5 or anuric.

drugRefs.dose: 40 mg SC once daily (adjust for renal function/weight)
drugRefs.why: HHS carries a very high thrombotic risk from hyperviscosity/dehydration; prophylactic LMWH is recommended unless contraindicated.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State
JBDS Management of the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults
ADA Standards of Care — Hyperglycaemic Crises

decision.label: Aggressive IV saline first, then low-rate insulin

confirm: Marked hyperglycaemia with high osmolality and minimal ketosis/acidosis, profound dehydration ± reduced consciousness (typically older T2DM).
